# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Welcome {#welcome}

*NavigatoR: Plotting Your Course Through R Fundamentals* guides you on an
explorative journey through the fundamentals of R programming. This book is
designed for anyone who wants to establish a reproducible workflow for their
data science work. From the basics of R to data manipulation and visualisation,
it provides a structured pathway to the essential skills.

You will start by setting up your R environment and understanding the core
concepts of the language. As you progress, you will learn how to manage
projects, organise data, and carry out robust analyses.

This book is not an exhaustive manual on every facet of R, nor is it a
statistics textbook. It is a curated guide, focused on the concepts and
techniques that matter most for getting real work done. It concentrates on the
*why* and *how* of setting up a robust workflow in R — the practical insights I
wish someone had given me when I started programming.

## How this book is organised

The book follows the structure of the course
**R: från datahantering till visualisering** at GIH, so each part corresponds to
a block of lectures. The book goes into more depth than the slides and adds
exercises; the two are meant to be used together.

| Part | Chapters | Corresponding lectures |
|------|----------|------------------------|
| **Getting started** | Installation, Positron, projects, basics, classes and objects, Quarto, version control | *Introduktion till R*, *Klasser och objekt*, *Quarto* |
| **Visualising data** | The grammar of graphics with `ggplot2` | *Datavisualisering* |
| **Getting data in and out** | Importing, exporting, file paths | *Importera och exportera data* |
| **Data wrangling** | Tidy data, `dplyr` verbs, pivoting, joins, strings and factors, cleaning | *Tidyverse verb*, *Pivoting*, *Joins*, *Städa data* |
| **Exploring and communicating** | EDA, tables, the full workflow | *Explorativ dataanalys*, *Tabeller* |
| **Beyond the basics** | Generative AI, writing functions and iteration, useful packages | *AI* |

You do not have to read it in order. If you are stuck on a specific problem, go
straight to the chapter that covers it — every chapter starts with a note saying
what it contains.

## How to use this book

::: {.callout-tip}
## Type the code, do not copy it
Every chapter is full of runnable code. You will learn considerably more by
typing it into your own R session, changing something, and seeing what breaks
than by reading it or pasting it. The typos you make are part of the process:
learning to read an error message is a skill in itself.
:::

Two kinds of exercise appear throughout:

**Quick checks** — self-marking questions that appear in boxes like this one:

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
Is this a self-marking question? `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`

What is `2 + 2`? `r webexercises::fitb(4)`
:::

Type or select an answer and the box tells you whether it is right. They exist
to catch misunderstandings early, not to be graded.

**Coding exercises** — longer tasks with a solution hidden behind a button:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise: an example

Calculate the mean of the numbers 4, 8 and 15.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
mean(c(4, 8, 15))
```

Try to write your own answer before opening the solution. Getting it wrong and
then seeing why is where most of the learning happens; reading the answer first
mostly produces the feeling of having understood it.
:::
:::

## Conventions

- Code uses the **native pipe** `|>` rather than `%>%`. They behave the same in
  almost all everyday use.
- Objects are assigned with `<-` and named in `snake_case`.
- Function names in the text are written as `mean()`, with parentheses.
- Package names are written as `dplyr`, and `package::function()` is used where
  it is helpful to show where a function comes from.
- Comments in code explain **why** a step is there, not what the line does
  mechanically.

::: {.callout-note}
## Package versions
R and the tidyverse move quickly, and this book uses current idioms rather than
the ones you will find in older tutorials. Where a function is recent, the text
says which version introduced it — for example `filter_out()` and
`recode_values()` need **dplyr 1.2.0** (@sec-dplyr).

If a function in this book does not exist on your machine, update the package
and check with `packageVersion("dplyr")`. If a function in someone else's code
does not exist any more, `news(package = "dplyr")` will usually tell you what
replaced it.
:::

## A note on data

The examples use built-in datasets — mostly `palmerpenguins` — so that every
piece of code in this book can be run by anyone, without downloading anything.

If you work with registry, clinical or otherwise identifiable data, two rules
apply from the very first line of code: never commit data files to Git, and
never paste identifiable data into an AI assistant or any other hosted service.
De-identify first. @sec-cleaning and @sec-workflow cover this in more detail.

::: {.callout-important}
## Tip
If anything in this book is unclear, using an AI assistant to explain or expand
on the topic is a good idea — as long as you check what it tells you against the
documentation. See @sec-ai.
:::
